statement: For every integer $k \ge 1$ there is a finite [triangle-free graph](c:triangle-free-graph) whose [chromatic number](c:chromatic-number) is $k$.

hypotheses.text: The number $k$ is a positive integer.

conclusion: Some finite graph $G_k$ has no triangle and satisfies $\chi(G_k) = k$.

proofs.name: Mycielski construction
proofs.slogan: Raise the chromatic number by one with the Mycielski graph, which creates no triangle, and start from an edge.
proofs.scope: All $k \ge 1$: $G_1$ is one vertex, $G_2$ is an edge, and $G_{k+1}$ is the Mycielski graph of $G_k$ for $k \ge 2$.

roles.why: The induction runs over the positive integer $k$, from the base graphs $G_1$ and $G_2$.

steps.slogan: Build the Mycielski graph $M(G)$ from a graph $G$ with vertices $v_1, \dots, v_n$.
steps.detail: Add new vertices $u_1, \dots, u_n$ and one more vertex $w$. Join $u_i$ to $v_j$ whenever $v_i v_j$ is an edge of $G$, and join $w$ to every $u_i$. The vertices $u_i$ are pairwise nonadjacent.

steps.slogan: Show that $M(G)$ is [triangle-free](c:triangle-free-graph) when $G$ is.
steps.detail: The neighbors of $w$ are the pairwise nonadjacent $u_i$, so $w$ lies in no triangle, and no triangle has two vertices $u_i$. A triangle with one $u_i$ and the vertices $v_j, v_l$ forces the triangle $v_i v_j v_l$ in $G$. A triangle inside the $v$'s lies in $G$.

steps.slogan: Extend a proper [coloring](c:graph-coloring) of $G$ to $M(G)$ with one new color.
steps.detail: Color $G$ with $c$ colors, give $u_i$ the color of $v_i$, and give $w$ the new color $c+1$. A vertex $u_i$ is adjacent to $v_j$ only when $v_i v_j$ is an edge of $G$, so the two colors differ. The neighbors of $w$ use colors at most $c$. Hence $\chi(M(G)) \le \chi(G) + 1$.

steps.slogan: Turn a proper coloring of $M(G)$ into one of $G$ with one color fewer.
steps.detail: Let $\varphi$ color $M(G)$ with $c$ colors and let $\varphi(w) = c$, so no $u_i$ has color $c$. Put $\psi(v_i) = \varphi(v_i)$ if $\varphi(v_i) \ne c$ and $\psi(v_i) = \varphi(u_i)$ otherwise. For an edge $v_i v_j$ with $\varphi(v_i) = c$, the vertex $u_i$ is adjacent to $v_j$, so $\psi(v_i) \ne \psi(v_j)$. Hence $\chi(G) \le c - 1$.

steps.slogan: Iterate the construction from an edge to reach every [chromatic number](c:chromatic-number).
steps.detail: The graphs $G_1$ (one vertex) and $G_2$ (an edge) are triangle-free with $\chi = 1$ and $\chi = 2$. If $G_k$ is triangle-free with $\chi(G_k) = k$, then $G_{k+1} = M(G_k)$ is triangle-free with $\chi = k + 1$ by the three steps above. Induction on $k$ finishes the proof.

concepts.c:triangle-free-graph: The construction must keep every graph in the sequence free of triangles.
concepts.c:chromatic-number: The construction raises this invariant by exactly one at each stage.
concepts.c:graph-coloring: Colorings of $G$ and of $M(G)$ are converted into each other.

source.note: Mycielski's construction, J. Mycielski, Sur le coloriage des graphes, Colloquium Mathematicum 3 (1955), 161-162.

statement: Let $f$ be [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) near the closed [annulus](c:annulus) $r_1 \le |z| \le r_3$ and let $M(r) = \max_{|z| = r} |f(z)|$. For $r_1 < r_2 < r_3$, $M(r_2)^{\log(r_3/r_1)} \le M(r_1)^{\log(r_3/r_2)} M(r_3)^{\log(r_2/r_1)}$. So $\log M(r)$ is convex in $\log r$ ([log-convexity](c:log-convexity)).

hypotheses.text: The radii satisfy $0 < r_1 < r_2 < r_3$, and the region is the closed [annulus](c:annulus) $r_1 \le |z| \le r_3$.
The function $f$ is [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) on an open set that contains the closed annulus.

conclusion: The three-circle inequality holds, that is, $\log M(r_2)$ lies below the chord of $\log M$ over $\log r_1$ and $\log r_3$.

proofs.name: Maximum modulus on z^p f^q
proofs.slogan: Bound a single-valued power $z^p f^q$ by the maximum modulus principle, then choose the exponent that balances the two outer circles.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. If $f \equiv 0$ both sides are $0$; otherwise $M(r) > 0$ for every $r$.

roles.why: The compact annulus has the two outer circles as its boundary, where the maximum modulus is read.
Holomorphy makes $z^p f^q$ holomorphic, and a zero set with a limit point forces $f \equiv 0$.

steps.slogan: Dispose of the case in which $f$ vanishes on a whole circle.
steps.detail: If $f$ vanishes on a circle $|z| = r$, its zeros have a limit point in the connected annulus $r_1 - \epsilon < |z| < r_3 + \epsilon$ (inside the domain for small $\epsilon$). The identity theorem gives $f \equiv 0$, and the inequality reads $0 \le 0$. Otherwise $M(r) > 0$ for all $r \in [r_1, r_3]$.

steps.slogan: Bound $z^p f^q$ on the annulus by its values on the two outer circles.
steps.detail: For integers $p$ and $q \ge 1$ the function $h = z^p f^q$ is single-valued and holomorphic near the annulus. The maximum modulus principle gives $|h| \le \max(r_1^p M(r_1)^q, r_3^p M(r_3)^q)$ on the annulus. Taking $q$-th roots, $r^a M(r) \le \max(r_1^a M(r_1), r_3^a M(r_3))$ for every rational $a = p/q$.

steps.slogan: Extend the bound from rational exponents to all real exponents.
steps.detail: Both sides of the inequality are continuous in $a$, and the rational numbers are dense in the real numbers. So $r^a M(r) \le \max(r_1^a M(r_1), r_3^a M(r_3))$ holds for every real $a$ and every $r \in [r_1, r_3]$.

steps.slogan: Choose the exponent $a$ that makes the two outer values equal.
steps.detail: Put $a = \log(M(r_1)/M(r_3)) / \log(r_3/r_1)$, so $r_1^a M(r_1) = r_3^a M(r_3)$. At $r = r_2$ the previous step gives $r_2^a M(r_2) \le r_1^a M(r_1)$, that is, $M(r_2) \le M(r_1)(r_1/r_2)^a$.

steps.slogan: Take logarithms and simplify to the three-circle inequality.
steps.detail: Taking logarithms, $\log M(r_2) \le \log M(r_1) - a\log(r_2/r_1)$. Substituting $a$ and using $\log(r_3/r_1) - \log(r_2/r_1) = \log(r_3/r_2)$ gives $\log M(r_2) \log(r_3/r_1) \le \log M(r_1) \log(r_3/r_2) + \log M(r_3) \log(r_2/r_1)$. This is the claim.

concepts.c:holomorphic-function: Holomorphy of $z^p f^q$ lets the maximum modulus principle apply.
concepts.c:annulus: The annulus is the compact region whose boundary circles carry the bound.
concepts.c:log-convexity: The inequality says exactly that $\log M$ is convex in $\log r$.

source.note: The classical maximum modulus proof; powers $z^p f^q$ with integer exponents avoid branches of $z^a$.

statement: Let $G$ be a [Lie group](c:lie-group) with [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) $\mathfrak g$ and let $X, Y \in \mathfrak g$. Then $\mathrm{Ad}_{\exp X}(Y) = e^{\mathrm{ad}_X}(Y) = \sum_{n \ge 0} \mathrm{ad}_X^n(Y)/n!$. For a matrix group this reads $e^X Y e^{-X} = \sum_{n\ge 0} \mathrm{ad}_X^n(Y)/n!$ with $\mathrm{ad}_X(Y) = XY - YX$.

hypotheses.text: $G$ is a [Lie group](c:lie-group) with Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$.
The elements $X$ and $Y$ lie in $\mathfrak g$.

conclusion: The operator $\mathrm{Ad}_{\exp X}$ on $\mathfrak g$ equals the operator exponential $e^{\mathrm{ad}_X}$, so $\mathrm{Ad}_{\exp X}(Y) = e^{\mathrm{ad}_X}(Y)$.

proofs.name: One-parameter group of operators
proofs.slogan: The operators $\mathrm{Ad}_{\exp tX}$ form a one-parameter group with generator $\mathrm{ad}_X$, so they equal $e^{t\,\mathrm{ad}_X}$.
proofs.scope: Any Lie group, so any matrix Lie group; for matrices $\mathrm{Ad}_g Y = gYg^{-1}$ and $\mathrm{ad}_X Y = XY - YX$. Real and complex Lie groups use the same argument.

roles.why: Smoothness and the homomorphism property of $\mathrm{Ad}$ make $t \mapsto \mathrm{Ad}_{\exp tX}$ a smooth one-parameter group.
The element $X$ defines the one-parameter subgroup, and $Y$ is the vector on which the operators act.

steps.slogan: Show that $\varphi(t) = \mathrm{Ad}_{\exp tX}$ is a smooth one-parameter group of operators on $\mathfrak g$.
steps.detail: The map $t \mapsto \exp(tX)$ is a smooth homomorphism $\mathbb R \to G$, and $\mathrm{Ad}\colon G \to GL(\mathfrak g)$ is a smooth homomorphism. So $\varphi(t+s) = \varphi(t)\varphi(s)$ and $\varphi(0) = I$.

steps.slogan: Compute the generator $\varphi'(0)$ as the operator $\mathrm{ad}_X$.
steps.detail: By definition $\mathrm{ad} = d\mathrm{Ad}_e$ is the derivative of $\mathrm{Ad}$ at the identity. The curve $\exp(tX)$ has velocity $X$ at $t = 0$, so the chain rule gives $\varphi'(0) = \mathrm{ad}_X$.

steps.slogan: Differentiate the group law to get the linear equation $\varphi'(t) = \varphi(t)\,\mathrm{ad}_X$.
steps.detail: Differentiate $\varphi(t+s) = \varphi(t)\varphi(s)$ in $s$ at $s = 0$. This gives $\varphi'(t) = \varphi(t)\varphi'(0) = \varphi(t)\,\mathrm{ad}_X$, with $\varphi(0) = I$.

steps.slogan: Solve the equation by uniqueness of solutions of linear differential equations.
steps.detail: The curve $t \mapsto e^{t\,\mathrm{ad}_X}$ solves the same [ordinary differential equation](c:ordinary-differential-equation) with the same value $I$ at $t = 0$. Solutions of linear equations with constant coefficients are unique, so $\varphi(t) = e^{t\,\mathrm{ad}_X}$.

steps.slogan: Set $t = 1$ and apply the operator to $Y$.
steps.detail: With $t = 1$, $\mathrm{Ad}_{\exp X} = e^{\mathrm{ad}_X}$, so $\mathrm{Ad}_{\exp X}(Y) = \sum_n \mathrm{ad}_X^n(Y)/n!$. For a matrix group $\mathrm{Ad}_{e^X} Y = e^X Y e^{-X}$, which gives the matrix form of the formula.

concepts.c:lie-group: The one-parameter subgroup $\exp(tX)$ and the map $\mathrm{Ad}$ live on the Lie group.
concepts.c:lie-algebra: The operators $\mathrm{ad}_X$ and $\mathrm{Ad}_g$ act on the Lie algebra.
concepts.c:ordinary-differential-equation: The group law turns the claim into a linear equation with a unique solution.

source.note: The standard one-parameter-group argument, as in B. C. Hall, Lie Groups, Lie Algebras, and Representations, chapter 3.

statement: If a type $A$ has [decidable equality](c:decidable-equality), then $A$ is an [h-set](c:h-set): for all $x, y : A$, any two elements of the [identity type](c:identity-type) $x = y$ are equal.

hypotheses.text: For all $x, y : A$ the proposition $x = y$ is decided, so $(x = y) + \neg(x = y)$ is inhabited.

conclusion: For all $x, y : A$ and $p, q : x = y$ there is an identification $p = q$.

proofs.name: Constant endomaps of identity types
proofs.slogan: Decidable equality gives a constant map on each identity type, and such a map forces every path to equal a fixed composite.
proofs.scope: Intensional type theory with path induction. The proof uses no axiom K, no univalence and no function extensionality.

roles.why: The decision for each pair $x, y$ defines the endomap $f_{xy}$ and its constancy.

steps.slogan: Define a map $f_{xy}\colon (x = y) \to (x = y)$ by cases on the decision.
steps.detail: Let $d(x,y)$ decide $x = y$. If $d(x,y) = \mathrm{inl}(r)$, put $f_{xy}(p) = r$. If $d(x,y) = \mathrm{inr}(n)$, put $f_{xy}(p) = \mathrm{ex\;falso}(n(p))$, which is defined because $n(p)$ is an element of the empty type.

steps.slogan: Show that $f_{xy}$ is constant: $f_{xy}(p) = f_{xy}(q)$ for all $p, q$.
steps.detail: If $d(x,y) = \mathrm{inl}(r)$, both values equal $r$. If $d(x,y) = \mathrm{inr}(n)$, then $n(p)$ is an element of the empty type, so every equation holds, including $f_{xy}(p) = f_{xy}(q)$.

steps.slogan: Prove $p = f_{xx}(\mathrm{refl}_x)^{-1} \cdot f_{xy}(p)$ for every path $p : x = y$ by path induction.
steps.detail: Fix $x$ and induct on $y$ and $p : x = y$. For $y = x$ and $p = \mathrm{refl}_x$ the claim reads $\mathrm{refl}_x = f_{xx}(\mathrm{refl}_x)^{-1} \cdot f_{xx}(\mathrm{refl}_x)$, which holds because a path cancels its inverse.

steps.slogan: Compare $p$ and $q$ through the common value $f_{xy}(p) = f_{xy}(q)$.
steps.detail: For $p, q : x = y$ the previous steps give $p = f_{xx}(\mathrm{refl}_x)^{-1} \cdot f_{xy}(p) = f_{xx}(\mathrm{refl}_x)^{-1} \cdot f_{xy}(q) = q$. So any two elements of $x = y$ are equal, and $A$ is an h-set.

concepts.c:decidable-equality: The decision on $x = y$ defines the endomap and shows that it is constant.
concepts.c:h-set: The conclusion says that every identity type of $A$ has at most one element.
concepts.c:identity-type: Path induction on the identity type proves the key identity for $p$.

source.note: Hedberg's argument via constant endofunctions of identity types, as in the HoTT book (Univalent Foundations Program, Homotopy Type Theory, section 7.2); first proved in M. Hedberg, J. Functional Programming 8 (1998), 413-436.

statement: Let $F_n$ and $F$ be [distribution functions](c:distribution-function) on $\mathbb R$ with $F_n(x) \to F(x)$ at every continuity point $x$ of $F$ ([convergence in distribution](c:convergence-in-distribution)). Then $\int g\,dF_n \to \int g\,dF$ for every [bounded continuous function](c:bounded-continuous-function) $g\colon \mathbb R \to \mathbb R$.

hypotheses.text: The functions $F_n$ and $F$ are [distribution functions](c:distribution-function): nondecreasing, right-continuous, with limits $0$ and $1$ at $-\infty$ and $+\infty$.
$F_n(x) \to F(x)$ at every continuity point $x$ of $F$.
The function $g$ is [bounded and continuous](c:bounded-continuous-function) on $\mathbb R$.

proofs.name: Approximation by step functions
proofs.slogan: Cut the line at continuity points of $F$, replace $g$ by a step function there, and control the tails and the step function separately.
proofs.scope: The forward direction on the real line. The converse (convergence of all $\int g\,dF_n$ implies weak convergence) follows by approximating indicators and is not proved here.

roles.why: Total mass one makes the tails small and gives the step sums the form of increments of $F_n$ and $F$.
Convergence at the chosen continuity points controls the tails and the step function.
Boundedness bounds the tails, and uniform continuity on $[a,b]$ gives the step approximation.

steps.slogan: Choose continuity points $a < b$ of $F$ that cut off small tails for every large $n$.
steps.detail: Let $K = \sup|g|$ and $\epsilon > 0$. The continuity points of $F$ are dense, so there are such points $a < b$ with $F(a) < \epsilon$ and $1 - F(b) < \epsilon$. Since $F_n(a) \to F(a)$ and $F_n(b) \to F(b)$, for $n \ge N_1$ we get $F_n(a) < \epsilon$ and $1 - F_n(b) < \epsilon$.

steps.slogan: Cut $[a, b]$ into cells at continuity points on which $g$ varies by less than $\epsilon$.
steps.detail: The function $g$ is uniformly continuous on $[a, b]$, so some $\delta > 0$ gives oscillation less than $\epsilon$ on every interval of length at most $\delta$. Dense continuity points give a partition $a = x_0 < \dots < x_m = b$ of mesh less than $\delta$, all of them continuity points of $F$.

steps.slogan: Compare $g$ with a step function $h$, with the same error for $F_n$ and $F$.
steps.detail: Let $h = \sum_i g(x_i)\mathbf 1_{(x_{i-1}, x_i]}$. For any distribution function $G$, $|\int g\,dG - \int h\,dG| \le \epsilon + K\,(G(a) + 1 - G(b))$, since $|g - h| < \epsilon$ on $(a,b]$ and $h = 0$ outside. So the error is at most $(1 + 2K)\epsilon$ for $G = F$ and for $G = F_n$ with $n \ge N_1$.

steps.slogan: Show that the integrals of the step function $h$ converge.
steps.detail: $\int h\,dF_n = \sum_i g(x_i)\,(F_n(x_i) - F_n(x_{i-1}))$ is a finite sum. Every $x_i$ is a continuity point of $F$, so the sum converges to $\int h\,dF$. Hence $|\int h\,dF_n - \int h\,dF| < \epsilon$ for $n \ge N_2$.

steps.slogan: Add the three errors and let $\epsilon$ tend to zero.
steps.detail: For $n \ge \max(N_1, N_2)$ the triangle inequality gives $|\int g\,dF_n - \int g\,dF| \le (1+2K)\epsilon + \epsilon + (1+2K)\epsilon = (3 + 4K)\epsilon$. Since $\epsilon$ is arbitrary, the integrals converge.

concepts.c:distribution-function: The increments of the distribution functions are the weights of the step sums.
concepts.c:convergence-in-distribution: Convergence at continuity points is the only input on $F_n$.
concepts.c:bounded-continuous-function: Boundedness controls the tails; continuity gives the step approximation.
concepts.c:uniformly-continuous-map: Uniform continuity on $[a,b]$ gives one cell size for all of $[a,b]$.

source.note: The classical Helly-Bray argument: approximate $g$ by a step function with jumps at continuity points of $F$.

statement: Let $X$ be a smooth projective [algebraic surface](c:algebraic-surface) over an algebraically closed field, $H$ an [ample divisor](c:ample-divisor), and $D$ a [divisor](c:divisor) with $D\cdot H = 0$ that is not numerically trivial. Then $D^2 < 0$. So the [intersection pairing](c:intersection-pairing) on $\mathrm{Num}(X)$ has signature $(1, \rho - 1)$.

hypotheses.text: $X$ is a smooth projective [algebraic surface](c:algebraic-surface) over an algebraically closed field.
$H$ is an [ample divisor](c:ample-divisor) on $X$.
The divisor $D$ satisfies $D \cdot H = 0$.
$D$ is not numerically trivial: $D \cdot E \ne 0$ for some divisor $E$.

conclusion: $D^2 < 0$, and the intersection form on $\mathrm{Num}(X)$, of rank $\rho$, is positive on $H$ and negative definite on $H^\perp$.

proofs.name: Riemann-Roch and ampleness
proofs.slogan: A class of positive square would be large by Riemann-Roch, which an ample divisor orthogonal to it forbids.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; $\mathrm{Num}(X)$ is a finitely generated free abelian group, of rank $\rho$. Write $h = H \cdot H > 0$ and let $K$ be the canonical divisor.

roles.why: Riemann-Roch, Serre duality and the intersection form exist on a smooth projective surface.
Ampleness gives $H \cdot C > 0$ for curves, $h > 0$, and the ample divisor $mH + D$.
$D \cdot H = 0$ keeps $nD$ orthogonal to $H$ and makes $(mH + D) \cdot (K - nD)$ tend to $-\infty$.
A divisor $E$ with $D \cdot E \ne 0$ lifts a zero square to a positive one, and $nD \sim 0$ is excluded.

steps.slogan: Replace $D$ by a class with $D \cdot H = 0$ and positive square.
steps.detail: Assume $D^2 \ge 0$ for contradiction. If $D^2 = 0$, take $E$ with $D \cdot E \ne 0$ and set $D' = h(nD + E) - (E \cdot H)H$, with $n$ an integer of the sign of $D \cdot E$. Then $D' \cdot H = 0$ and $D'^2 = h^2(2n\,D \cdot E + E^2) - h(E \cdot H)^2 > 0$ for $|n|$ large. Rename $D'$ as $D$.

steps.slogan: Count sections of $nD$ with Riemann-Roch and Serre duality.
steps.detail: Riemann-Roch gives $\chi(nD) = \chi(\mathcal O_X) + \tfrac12 n^2 D^2 - \tfrac12 n\,D \cdot K$, and Serre duality gives $h^2(nD) = h^0(K - nD)$. Since $\chi \le h^0 + h^2$ and $D^2 > 0$, $h^0(nD) + h^0(K - nD) \to \infty$. So for every large $n$, $nD$ or $K - nD$ is linearly equivalent to an effective divisor.

steps.slogan: Exclude the case that $nD$ is linearly equivalent to an effective divisor.
steps.detail: If $nD \sim E \ge 0$, then $E \cdot H = nD \cdot H = 0$. An ample divisor meets every curve positively, so $E = 0$, hence $nD \sim 0$ and $D^2 = 0$, against $D^2 > 0$. So $K - nD$ is effective up to linear equivalence for every large $n$.

steps.slogan: Test the effective class $K - nD$ against the ample divisor $mH + D$ to contradict $D^2 > 0$.
steps.detail: For $m$ large, $A = mH + D$ is ample, so $A \cdot (K - nD) \ge 0$ for every large $n$. But $A \cdot (K - nD) = m\,H \cdot K + D \cdot K - nD^2$, using $H \cdot D = 0$, and this tends to $-\infty$ as $n \to \infty$. So $D^2 > 0$ is impossible, and $D^2 < 0$.

steps.slogan: Read off the signature of the intersection form on $\mathrm{Num}(X)$.
steps.detail: Write $v = \frac{v \cdot H}{h}H + w$ with $w \in H^\perp$, so $\mathrm{Num}(X)_{\mathbb R} = \mathbb R H \oplus H^\perp$. The form is negative on rational points of $H^\perp$, so negative semidefinite on $H^\perp$ by continuity. It is nondegenerate on $H^\perp$ because it is nondegenerate on $\mathrm{Num}(X)$ and $h \ne 0$, so it is negative definite there. The signature is $(1, \rho - 1)$.

concepts.c:algebraic-surface: Riemann-Roch and Serre duality on the surface count the sections of $nD$.
concepts.c:ample-divisor: Ampleness makes intersection numbers with curves positive and bounds the effective class.
concepts.c:divisor: The proof studies the class $D$, its multiples $nD$ and the effective divisors in them.
concepts.c:intersection-pairing: The signature statement describes this form on divisor classes.

source.note: Riemann-Roch proof in the style of Hartshorne, Algebraic Geometry, chapter V, theorem 1.9; the reduction and the final test against $mH + D$ are written out here.

statement: Let $X$ and $Y$ be [Riemann surfaces](c:riemann-surface) with $X$ [connected](c:connected-space), and let $f, g\colon X \to Y$ be [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) maps. If $f = g$ on a set $A \subseteq X$ that has a [limit point](c:limit-point) in $X$, then $f = g$ on $X$.

hypotheses.text: $X$ and $Y$ are [Riemann surfaces](c:riemann-surface).
The surface $X$ is [connected](c:connected-space).
The maps $f, g\colon X \to Y$ are [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function).
$f = g$ on a set $A \subseteq X$ that has a [limit point](c:limit-point) $p_0 \in X$.

proofs.name: Open and closed agreement set
proofs.slogan: The set of points near which $f$ and $g$ agree is open, closed and nonempty, so connectedness makes it all of $X$.
proofs.scope: All holomorphic maps between Riemann surfaces; for $Y = \mathbb C$ these are holomorphic functions. The planar identity theorem is the local input.

roles.why: Charts of $X$ and $Y$ reduce the local question to the plane, and $Y$ is Hausdorff.
A nonempty open and closed subset of a connected space is the whole space.
Continuity gives equal values at a limit point, and holomorphy lets the planar identity theorem act in charts.
The limit point $p_0$ of the agreement set is the first point of $S$.

steps.slogan: Show that $f$ and $g$ take equal values at a limit point of an agreement set.
steps.detail: Let $B \subseteq X$ be a set with $f = g$ on $B$, and let $p \in X$ be a limit point of $B$. Take $b_n \in B \setminus \{p\}$ with $b_n \to p$. Then $f(p) = \lim f(b_n) = \lim g(b_n) = g(p)$, because $Y$ is Hausdorff and limits are unique.

steps.slogan: Pass to charts at $p$ and apply the planar identity theorem.
steps.detail: Choose a chart $\psi$ of $Y$ at $f(p) = g(p)$ and a connected coordinate disc $U \ni p$ with $f(U), g(U)$ in the chart. The functions $\psi \circ f$ and $\psi \circ g$ are holomorphic on $U$ and agree on $B \cap U$, which accumulates at $p$. So they agree on $U$, and $f = g$ on the neighborhood $U$ of $p$.

steps.slogan: Define the set $S$ of points with a neighborhood of agreement and show that it is nonempty.
steps.detail: Let $S = \{x \in X : f = g \text{ on a neighborhood of } x\}$. It is open by definition. The limit point $p_0$ of $A$ lies in $S$ by the previous step with $B = A$.

steps.slogan: Show that $S$ contains each of its limit points, so $S$ is closed.
steps.detail: Since $f = g$ on $S$, the set $S$ is an agreement set. Let $q \in X$ be a limit point of $S$. By the local step with $B = S$, $q \in S$. So $S$ contains its limit points and is closed in $X$.

steps.slogan: Conclude $S = X$ from the connectedness of $X$.
steps.detail: The set $S$ is nonempty, open and closed in the connected space $X$, so $S = X$. Hence $f = g$ near every point, and so $f = g$ on $X$.

concepts.c:riemann-surface: Charts of the surfaces turn the local question into a planar one.
concepts.c:connected-space: Connectedness spreads agreement from one open and closed set to all of $X$.
concepts.c:holomorphic-function: Holomorphy in charts lets the planar identity theorem apply.
concepts.c:limit-point: A limit point of an agreement set is where agreement becomes local.

source.note: The standard open-closed argument, as in O. Forster, Lectures on Riemann Surfaces, theorem 1.11.

statement: Let $s(n) \ge \log n$ be space-constructible. If a language $L$ is decided by a [nondeterministic Turing machine](c:nondeterministic-turing-machine) in space $O(s(n))$, then its complement is also decided by one in space $O(s(n))$. So $\mathrm{NSPACE}(s) = \mathrm{coNSPACE}(s)$.

hypotheses.text: The function $s(n) \ge \log n$ is space-constructible.
A [nondeterministic Turing machine](c:nondeterministic-turing-machine) $M$ decides $L$ in space $s(n)$.

conclusion: Some nondeterministic machine decides the complement of $L$ in [space](c:nondeterministic-space) $O(s(n))$.

proofs.name: Inductive counting
proofs.slogan: Count the configurations reachable in at most $i$ steps, level by level, and then certify that no accepting configuration is reachable.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for constructible $s$; the case $s(n) = \log n$ is $\mathrm{NL} = \mathrm{coNL}$. A bound $O(s)$ is the same as $s$ after a change of the work alphabet.

roles.why: Constructibility lets the algorithm lay out $O(s)$ cells, and $s \ge \log n$ lets it address input positions and write counters.
The machine $M$ defines the [configuration](c:cfg) graph in which reachability is decided.

steps.slogan: Reduce acceptance by $M$ to reachability in its [configuration](c:cfg) graph.
steps.detail: On input $x$, the configurations of $M$ that use at most $s(|x|)$ cells form a graph with $N = 2^{O(s(|x|))}$ nodes, each coded in $O(s(|x|))$ bits. We may assume one accepting configuration $c_{acc}$. Then $x \in L$ if and only if $c_{acc}$ is reachable from the start configuration $c_0$.

steps.slogan: Name the sets $R_i$ of nodes reachable in at most $i$ steps and their sizes $c_i$.
steps.detail: Let $R_i$ be the set of nodes reachable from $c_0$ in at most $i$ steps, and $c_i = |R_i|$, for $0 \le i \le N$. Then $c_0 = 1$ and each $c_i \le N$ fits in $O(s)$ bits. The goal is to decide $c_{acc} \notin R_N$.

steps.slogan: Certify that a node lies in $R_i$ by guessing a path.
steps.detail: To check $v \in R_i$, guess a path $c_0 = v_0, v_1, \dots, v_j = v$ with $j \le i$, step by step, keeping only the current node and a step counter. This uses $O(s)$ space, and some branch accepts if and only if $v \in R_i$.

steps.slogan: Compute $c_{i+1}$ from $c_i$ by listing the members of $R_i$ in order.
steps.detail: For each node $v$, run over all nodes $u$ in order. Guess whether $u \in R_i$; if yes, verify it, increase a counter, and mark $v$ if $u = v$ or $u \to v$. If the counter differs from $c_i$ at the end, reject. Otherwise all of $R_i$ was listed, so the mark is correct, and the number of marked $v$ is $c_{i+1}$. Each branch rejects or returns the true $c_{i+1}$, and some branch returns it.

steps.slogan: List $R_N$ once more and accept if the target never appears.
steps.detail: Starting with $c_0 = 1$, compute $c_1, \dots, c_N$ with the previous step. Then list $R_N$ in the same way and reject if $c_{acc}$ is verified. A branch that ends with counter $c_N$ has verified $c_N$ distinct members of $R_N$, which is all of $R_N$. So the machine accepts if and only if $c_{acc} \notin R_N$, in space $O(s)$.

concepts.c:nondeterministic-turing-machine: Guessing paths and memberships is the only nondeterminism that the algorithm needs.
concepts.c:nondeterministic-space: The algorithm shows that the complement lies in the same space class.
concepts.c:cfg: Nodes of the graph are configurations, and counting them in $O(s)$ cells is the key.

source.note: Inductive counting, as in M. Sipser, Introduction to the Theory of Computation, theorem 8.27; original proofs: N. Immerman, SIAM J. Comput. 17 (1988), 935-938, and R. Szelepcsenyi, Acta Informatica 26 (1988), 279-284.

proofs.name: Arctangent addition formula
proofs.slogan: Double $\arctan\frac15$ twice to get $\arctan\frac{120}{119}$, which equals $\arctan 1 + \arctan\frac1{239}$.
proofs.scope: The whole identity for real arctangent; all arguments of the addition formula have product less than one.

steps.slogan: Prove $\arctan x + \arctan y = \arctan\frac{x+y}{1-xy}$ when $xy < 1$.
steps.detail: Put $\alpha = \arctan x$ and $\beta = \arctan y$, so $\alpha + \beta \in (-\pi, \pi)$. Then $\cos(\alpha+\beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta\,(1 - xy) > 0$, so $\alpha + \beta \in (-\pi/2, \pi/2)$. The tangent addition formula gives $\tan(\alpha+\beta) = \frac{x+y}{1-xy}$, and $\arctan$ inverts $\tan$ on $(-\pi/2, \pi/2)$.

steps.slogan: Set $y = x$ to double an [arctangent](c:arctangent): $2\arctan x = \arctan\frac{2x}{1-x^2}$ for $|x| < 1$.
steps.detail: For $|x| < 1$ we have $x \cdot x < 1$, so the addition formula with $y = x$ applies and gives the doubling formula.

steps.slogan: Double $\arctan\frac15$ twice to get $\arctan\frac{120}{119}$.
steps.detail: With $x = \frac15$, $2\arctan\frac15 = \arctan\frac{2/5}{24/25} = \arctan\frac5{12}$. Since $\frac5{12} < 1$, doubling again gives $2\arctan\frac5{12} = \arctan\frac{5/6}{119/144} = \arctan\frac{120}{119}$. So $4\arctan\frac15 = \arctan\frac{120}{119}$.

steps.slogan: Write $\frac\pi4$ as $\arctan 1$ and add $\arctan\frac1{239}$ to it.
steps.detail: Since $\tan\frac\pi4 = 1$ and $\frac\pi4 \in (-\frac\pi2, \frac\pi2)$, $\arctan 1 = \frac\pi4$. As $1 \cdot \frac1{239} < 1$, the addition formula gives $\frac\pi4 + \arctan\frac1{239} = \arctan\frac{240/239}{238/239} = \arctan\frac{120}{119}$.

steps.slogan: Compare the two expressions for $\arctan\frac{120}{119}$ and rearrange.
steps.detail: The two previous steps give $4\arctan\frac15 = \arctan\frac{120}{119} = \frac\pi4 + \arctan\frac1{239}$. Subtracting $\arctan\frac1{239}$ gives $4\arctan\frac15 - \arctan\frac1{239} = \frac\pi4$.

concepts.c:arctangent: The identity and every step concern the inverse tangent and its addition formula.

source.note: mathlib doubles twice with Real.two_mul_arctan, rewrites pi/4 as Real.arctan_one, and closes with Real.arctan_add and norm_num.

statement: For $0 \le x \le \pi/2$, the [sine function](c:sine-function) satisfies $\frac{2}{\pi}x \le \sin x \le x$.

hypotheses.text: The real number $x$ satisfies $0 \le x \le \pi/2$.

conclusion: Both $\frac{2}{\pi}x \le \sin x$ and $\sin x \le x$ hold.

formal.difference: The declaration proves only the lower bound. The upper bound $\sin x \le x$ is the separate declaration Real.sin_le.

proofs.name: Concavity of sine
proofs.slogan: Sine lies above its chord from $0$ to $\pi/2$ by concavity, and below the line $y = x$ because its derivative is at most one.
proofs.scope: The whole inequality on $[0, \pi/2]$; equality holds at $x = 0$, and the lower bound is also an equality at $x = \pi/2$.

roles.why: The range makes $2x/\pi$ a convex weight in $[0, 1]$ and keeps $x \ge 0$ for the integral bound.

steps.slogan: Show that sine is [concave](c:concavity) on $[0, \pi]$.
steps.detail: On $[0, \pi]$ we have $\sin t \ge 0$, so $(\sin)'' = -\sin \le 0$ there. A function with nonpositive second derivative is concave.

steps.slogan: Compare sine with the [chord](c:chord) through $(0, 0)$ and $(\pi/2, 1)$.
steps.detail: For $t \in [0, 1]$ the point $t\pi/2$ is the convex combination of $0$ and $\pi/2$ with weights $1 - t$ and $t$. Concavity gives $\sin(t\pi/2) \ge (1 - t)\sin 0 + t\sin(\pi/2) = t$.

steps.slogan: Substitute $t = 2x/\pi$ to get the lower bound.
steps.detail: For $0 \le x \le \pi/2$ the number $t = 2x/\pi$ lies in $[0, 1]$. The chord inequality becomes $\sin x \ge 2x/\pi$.

steps.slogan: Bound the sine by integrating $\cos t \le 1$ from $0$ to $x$.
steps.detail: For $x \ge 0$, $\sin x = \int_0^x \cos t\,dt \le \int_0^x 1\,dt = x$.

steps.slogan: Join the lower and the upper bound on the same interval.
steps.detail: The lower bound of step 3 and the upper bound of step 4 hold for the same $x \in [0, \pi/2]$, so $\frac{2}{\pi}x \le \sin x \le x$.

concepts.c:sine-function: The inequality compares the sine with two linear functions.
concepts.c:concavity: Concavity puts the graph of sine above its chord.
concepts.c:chord: The chord from $0$ to $\pi/2$ is the linear lower bound.

source.note: mathlib proves the lower bound in Real.le_sin_mul by concavity of sine on [0, pi] (strictConcaveOn_sin_Icc), then rescales; it proves the upper bound separately in Real.sin_le.

statement: Let $H_1$ and $H_2$ be [Hilbert spaces](c:hilbert-space), $U \subseteq H_1$, and $f\colon U \to H_2$ an $L$-[Lipschitz](c:lipschitz-function) map. Then $f$ extends to an $L$-Lipschitz map $F\colon H_1 \to H_2$.

hypotheses.text: $H_1$ and $H_2$ are [Hilbert spaces](c:hilbert-space).
$U$ is any subset of $H_1$.
The map $f\colon U \to H_2$ is $L$-[Lipschitz](c:lipschitz-function): $\|f(x) - f(y)\| \le L\|x - y\|$.

conclusion: A map $F\colon H_1 \to H_2$ has $F|_U = f$ and $\|F(x) - F(y)\| \le L\|x - y\|$ for all $x, y \in H_1$.

proofs.name: Intersecting balls and Zorn
proofs.slogan: Extend by one point at a time: finitely many balls meet by a minimax argument, all balls meet by weak compactness, and Zorn's lemma finishes.
proofs.scope: Real Hilbert spaces of any dimension; a complex space is treated as a real one. The proof takes $L = 1$ after scaling.

roles.why: The inner product gives the variance identity, and reflexivity makes closed balls weakly compact.
The pair $(U, f)$ is the starting point of the Zorn argument.
The estimate $\|f(x_i) - f(x_j)\| \le L\|x_i - x_j\|$ is what bounds the ratio $t$ by $1$.

steps.slogan: Reduce to the case that $f$ is $1$-Lipschitz and $U$ is nonempty.
steps.detail: If $L = 0$ or $U = \emptyset$, a constant map extends $f$. Otherwise extend the $1$-Lipschitz map $f/L$ and multiply the extension by $L$.

steps.slogan: Minimize the largest ratio of distance to radius over finitely many image points.
steps.detail: Let $x \in H_1 \setminus U$, let $x_1, \dots, x_k \in U$, $y_i = f(x_i)$ and $r_i = \|x - x_i\| > 0$. The function $\phi(y) = \max_i \|y - y_i\|/r_i$ is continuous and coercive on the finite-dimensional span of the $y_i$, so it has a minimizer $y^*$ with minimum value $t$.

steps.slogan: Extract convex weights that balance the active constraints at the minimizer.
steps.detail: Let $I$ be the set of $i$ with $\|y^* - y_i\| = t r_i$. If $t = 0$ then $t \le 1$ is clear. If $t > 0$, then $0$ lies in the convex hull of the gradients $(y^* - y_i)/(t r_i^2)$, $i \in I$, so there are weights $\lambda_i \ge 0$, $\sum\lambda_i = 1$, with $y^* = \sum \lambda_i y_i$.

steps.slogan: Compare the weighted spreads of the image points and of the domain points.
steps.detail: For $y^* = \sum \lambda_i y_i$: $\sum_{i,j}\lambda_i\lambda_j\|y_i - y_j\|^2 = 2\sum\lambda_i\|y_i - y^*\|^2 = 2t^2\sum\lambda_i r_i^2$. Likewise $\sum_{i,j}\lambda_i\lambda_j\|x_i - x_j\|^2 \le 2\sum\lambda_i\|x_i - x\|^2 = 2\sum\lambda_i r_i^2$. Since $\|y_i - y_j\| \le \|x_i - x_j\|$, we get $t \le 1$, so $\|y^* - y_i\| \le r_i$ for all $i$.

steps.slogan: Pass from finitely many balls to all balls by weak compactness.
steps.detail: For $u \in U$ let $B_u$ be the closed [ball](c:ball) with center $f(u)$ and radius $\|x - u\|$. It is convex and closed, so closed in the [weak topology](c:weak-topology), and lies in one weakly compact ball (Banach-Alaoglu; a Hilbert space is reflexive). Any finitely many $B_u$ meet by the finite case, so some $y_x$ lies in all $B_u$. Then $\|y_x - f(u)\| \le \|x - u\|$ for all $u \in U$.

steps.slogan: Extend to all of $H_1$ with Zorn's lemma.
steps.detail: Order the pairs $(V, g)$, with $U \subseteq V \subseteq H_1$ and $g$ a $1$-Lipschitz extension of $f$, by extension. A union of a chain is an upper bound, so a maximal pair $(V, g)$ exists. If $V \ne H_1$, pick $x \notin V$; the previous step applied to $g$ on $V$ gives a $1$-Lipschitz extension to $V \cup \{x\}$, against maximality. So $V = H_1$.

concepts.c:hilbert-space: The inner product gives the variance identity and the weak compactness of balls.
concepts.c:lipschitz-function: The Lipschitz bound on $f$ is the hypothesis that the extension must keep.
concepts.c:ball: The extension value must lie in every ball around an image point.
concepts.c:weak-topology: Weak compactness of balls turns finitely many common points into one.

source.note: Kirszbraun's theorem (Fund. Math. 22 (1934), 77-108; Valentine, Amer. J. Math. 67 (1945), 83-93); the finite case here is by a minimization argument.

statement: Take a steady, incompressible, irrotational, inviscid plane flow of density $\rho$ outside a body with piecewise smooth boundary $C$. Let it be tangent to $C$ and tend to $V > 0$ along the $x$-axis at infinity, with [circulation](c:circulation) $\Gamma = \oint_C (u\,dx + v\,dy)$ (counterclockwise). Then the force per unit span on the body is $(F_x, F_y) = (0, -\rho V \Gamma)$.

hypotheses.text: The flow is steady, incompressible, irrotational and inviscid with density $\rho$ outside the body, so $dw/dz = u - iv$ is holomorphic there.
The velocity is tangent to the boundary $C$.
The velocity tends to $V > 0$ along the $x$-axis at infinity.

conclusion: $F_x = 0$ and $F_y = -\rho V \Gamma$, so the force is perpendicular to the stream and has magnitude $\rho V |\Gamma|$.

proofs.name: Blasius law and residues
proofs.slogan: Write the pressure force as a contour integral by Bernoulli's law, move the contour to infinity, and read the residue.
proofs.scope: The classical two-dimensional model with given circulation; the Kutta condition that fixes $\Gamma$ for an airfoil is not part of the statement. The curve $C$ is counterclockwise.

roles.why: Bernoulli's law gives the pressure, and holomorphy of $dw/dz$ allows the contour move and the Laurent series.
Tangency turns $|u|^2\,d\bar z$ into $(dw/dz)^2\,dz$ and makes the flux through $C$ zero.
The limit $V$ at infinity is the constant term of the Laurent series.

steps.slogan: Express the pressure force through Bernoulli's law as an integral of $|u|^2$.
steps.detail: For this flow $p = p_0 - \tfrac12\rho|u|^2$ with constant $p_0$. The force is $-\oint_C p\,\mathbf n\,ds$ with $\mathbf n\,ds = (dy, -dx)$. So $F_x - iF_y = -i\oint_C p\,d\bar z = \tfrac{i\rho}{2}\oint_C |u|^2\,d\bar z$, because the constant $p_0$ integrates to $0$.

steps.slogan: Turn the integral into $\oint_C (dw/dz)^2\,dz$ by tangency.
steps.detail: On $C$ the velocity $u + iv = q e^{i\theta}$ is parallel to $dz = e^{i\theta}|dz|$. So $(u - iv)^2\,dz = q^2 e^{-i\theta}|dz| = |u|^2\,d\bar z$. Hence $F_x - iF_y = \tfrac{i\rho}{2}\oint_C (dw/dz)^2\,dz$, which is Blasius's law.

steps.slogan: Move the [contour integral](c:contour-integral) from $C$ to a large circle.
steps.detail: The function $(dw/dz)^2$ is holomorphic between $C$ and the circle $|z| = R$. Cauchy's integral theorem gives $\oint_C = \oint_{|z| = R}$, both counterclockwise.

steps.slogan: Expand $dw/dz$ in a [Laurent series](c:laurent-series) at infinity and read its first two coefficients.
steps.detail: Outside a disc, $dw/dz = a_0 + a_1/z + a_2/z^2 + \cdots$, and $a_0 = V$ by the condition at infinity. Also $2\pi i\,a_1 = \oint_C (u - iv)(dx + i\,dy) = \Gamma + i\oint_C (u\,dy - v\,dx)$. The last integral is the flux through $C$, which is $0$ by tangency, so $a_1 = \Gamma/(2\pi i)$.

steps.slogan: Compute the integral with the [residue](c:residue) of $(dw/dz)^2$.
steps.detail: $(dw/dz)^2 = V^2 + 2Va_1/z + O(z^{-2})$, so the coefficient of $1/z$ is $2Va_1 = V\Gamma/(\pi i)$. The residue theorem gives $\oint_{|z| = R}(dw/dz)^2\,dz = 2V\Gamma$. Hence $F_x - iF_y = \tfrac{i\rho}{2}\cdot 2V\Gamma = i\rho V\Gamma$, so $F_x = 0$ and $F_y = -\rho V\Gamma$.

concepts.c:circulation: The circulation $\Gamma$ is the coefficient that the residue picks out.
concepts.c:contour-integral: The force is a contour integral, and Cauchy's theorem moves the contour.
concepts.c:laurent-series: The Laurent series at infinity holds the stream speed and the circulation.
concepts.c:residue: The residue of $(dw/dz)^2$ at infinity gives the whole force.

source.note: Blasius's law and the residue theorem, the textbook derivation as in L. M. Milne-Thomson, Theoretical Hydrodynamics.

statement: Let $p$ be a [prime number](c:prime-number) and $f \in \mathbb Z[x]$ a [polynomial](c:polynomial) of degree $n$ with some coefficient not divisible by $p$. Then the [congruence](c:polynomial-congruence) $f(x) \equiv 0 \pmod p$ has at most $n$ solutions modulo $p$.

hypotheses.text: $p$ is a [prime number](c:prime-number).
$f \in \mathbb Z[x]$ has degree $n$, and some coefficient of $f$ is not divisible by $p$.

conclusion: At most $n$ residue classes $x$ modulo $p$ satisfy $f(x) \equiv 0 \pmod p$.

proofs.name: Roots over a field
proofs.slogan: Reduce modulo $p$ to a nonzero polynomial over the field $\mathbb F_p$, and bound its roots by its degree through the factor theorem.
proofs.scope: Every $n \ge 0$, with a prime modulus. For a composite modulus the bound fails: $x^2 \equiv 1 \pmod 8$ has four solutions.

roles.why: Primality makes $\mathbb Z/p$ a field, hence an integral domain, where a product vanishes only if a factor does.
A coefficient not divisible by $p$ makes the reduction nonzero, with degree at most $n$.

steps.slogan: Reduce $f$ modulo $p$ to a nonzero polynomial over the field $\mathbb F_p$.
steps.detail: Since $p$ is prime, $\mathbb F_p = \mathbb Z/p$ is a [field](c:field). The reduction $\bar f$ is nonzero because some coefficient is not divisible by $p$, and its degree $m$ satisfies $m \le n$. Solutions modulo $p$ are exactly the roots of $\bar f$ in $\mathbb F_p$.

steps.slogan: Split a linear factor $x - a$ off a polynomial at a [root](c:root-of-a-polynomial) $a$.
steps.detail: Let $g \ne 0$ have degree $m \ge 1$ over a field, with a root $a$. Division with remainder gives $g = (x - a)q + r$ with $r$ constant, and evaluation at $a$ gives $r = 0$. So $g = (x - a)q$ with $q \ne 0$ of degree $m - 1$.

steps.slogan: Prove by induction on $m$ that a nonzero polynomial of degree $m$ over a field has at most $m$ roots.
steps.detail: For $m = 0$ the polynomial is a nonzero constant with no root. For $m \ge 1$ take a root $a$ (if none, we are done) and write $g = (x - a)q$. A root $b \ne a$ gives $(b - a)q(b) = 0$, so $q(b) = 0$ because a field is an [integral domain](c:integral-domain). By induction $q$ has at most $m - 1$ roots, so $g$ has at most $m$.

steps.slogan: Combine the root bound with the reduction to count the solutions.
steps.detail: The reduction $\bar f$ is nonzero of degree $m \le n$, so it has at most $m \le n$ roots in $\mathbb F_p$. Hence the congruence has at most $n$ solutions modulo $p$.

concepts.c:prime-number: A prime modulus makes the residues modulo $p$ a field.
concepts.c:polynomial: The proof counts the roots of the polynomial by its degree.
concepts.c:polynomial-congruence: Solutions of the congruence are exactly the roots of the reduced polynomial.
concepts.c:field: Division with remainder and the absence of zero divisors need a field.
concepts.c:root-of-a-polynomial: Each root gives a linear factor that lowers the degree by one.
concepts.c:integral-domain: A product vanishes only if a factor vanishes, so other roots pass to the quotient.

source.note: The standard proof by induction on the degree through the factor theorem over the field F_p.

statement: Let $K$ be a [number field](c:number-field) and let $\pi_K(x)$ count the prime ideals of $\mathcal O_K$ of norm at most $x$. Then $\pi_K(x) \sim x/\log x$ as $x \to \infty$.

hypotheses.text: $K$ is a [number field](c:number-field), a finite extension of $\mathbb Q$ of degree $n$.

proofs.name: Dedekind zeta function and a Tauberian step
proofs.slogan: Continue the Dedekind zeta function past its pole at one, show that it has no zero on the line $\mathrm{Re}\,s = 1$, and convert this into prime ideal counts.
proofs.scope: An outline: each analytic step rests on Landau's paper. For $K = \mathbb Q$ it is the prime number theorem, and the same route covers every number field.

roles.why: The finite degree $n$ gives the lattice-point error term and the factorization of ideals that define $\zeta_K$.

steps.slogan: Define the [Dedekind zeta function](c:dedekind-zeta-function) and its [Euler product](c:euler-product).
steps.detail: For $\mathrm{Re}\,s > 1$ put $\zeta_K(s) = \sum_{\mathfrak a} N\mathfrak a^{-s}$ over the nonzero ideals. Unique factorization of ideals gives the product $\prod_{\mathfrak p}(1 - N\mathfrak p^{-s})^{-1}$, and the series converges absolutely.

steps.slogan: Continue $\zeta_K$ past $\mathrm{Re}\,s = 1$ and find a simple pole at $s = 1$.
steps.detail: Landau counts the ideals of norm at most $x$ in each ideal class as lattice points in a region, and gets $\kappa x + O(x^{1 - 1/n})$. So $\zeta_K$ continues meromorphically to $\mathrm{Re}\,s > 1 - 1/n$, with a simple pole at $s = 1$ whose residue $\kappa$ the class number formula gives.

steps.slogan: Show that $\zeta_K$ has no zero on the line $\mathrm{Re}\,s = 1$.
steps.detail: The Euler product gives $\log|\zeta_K(s)| = \mathrm{Re}\sum_{\mathfrak p, k} N\mathfrak p^{-ks}/k$. With $3 + 4\cos\theta + \cos 2\theta \ge 0$ this yields $|\zeta_K(\sigma)^3\,\zeta_K(\sigma + it)^4\,\zeta_K(\sigma + 2it)| \ge 1$ for $\sigma > 1$. A zero at $1 + it$, $t \ne 0$, would drive the left side to $0$ as $\sigma \to 1^+$.

steps.slogan: Pass to the logarithmic derivative, a Dirichlet series with nonnegative coefficients.
steps.detail: For $\mathrm{Re}\,s > 1$, $-\zeta_K'(s)/\zeta_K(s) = \sum_{\mathfrak a}\Lambda_K(\mathfrak a)N\mathfrak a^{-s}$, with $\Lambda_K(\mathfrak p^k) = \log N\mathfrak p$ and $0$ elsewhere. By the two previous steps it is analytic on $\mathrm{Re}\,s \ge 1$ except for a simple pole at $s = 1$ with residue $1$.

steps.slogan: Convert the pole at $s = 1$ into an asymptotic for the summatory function.
steps.detail: The coefficients $\sum_{N\mathfrak a = k}\Lambda_K(\mathfrak a)$ are nonnegative, so the Wiener-Ikehara theorem gives $\psi_K(x) = \sum_{N\mathfrak a \le x}\Lambda_K(\mathfrak a) \sim x$. Landau reaches the same conclusion by contour integration.

steps.slogan: Remove prime powers and higher-degree primes, then sum by parts to reach $\pi_K(x)$.
steps.detail: At most $n$ prime ideals lie over each rational prime, so prime powers and prime ideals of degree at least $2$ contribute $o(x)$ to $\psi_K(x)$. Hence $\sum_{N\mathfrak p \le x}\log N\mathfrak p \sim x$, and partial summation gives $\pi_K(x) \sim x/\log x$, as in the derivation of the prime number theorem from $\psi(x) \sim x$.

concepts.c:number-field: The field fixes the ideals counted and the degree $n$ in the error term.
concepts.c:dedekind-zeta-function: Its pole and its zero-free line control the count of prime ideals.
concepts.c:euler-product: The Euler product links the zeta function to the prime ideals and shows nonvanishing.

source.ref: E. Landau, Neuer Beweis des Primzahlsatzes und Beweis des Primidealsatzes, Mathematische Annalen 56 (1903), 645-670
source.note: Landau proves the theorem by this route; the Tauberian step is stated here with the Wiener-Ikehara theorem.

statement: Let $T$ be a [Lawvere theory](c:lawvere-theory), $\mathrm{Mod}(T)$ its category of models, and $U(M) = M(1)$ the [forgetful functor](c:forgetful-functor). Then $\Phi\colon T(n, m) \to \mathrm{Nat}(U^n, U^m)$, $t \mapsto (M \mapsto M(t))$, is a bijection compatible with composition. So the [algebraic theory](c:algebraic-theory) $T$ is recovered from $U$.

hypotheses.text: $T$ is a small category with finite products whose objects are the powers $n = 1^n$ of one object $1$ (a [Lawvere theory](c:lawvere-theory)).
$\mathrm{Mod}(T)$ is the category of finite-product-preserving functors $T \to \mathbf{Set}$, and $U(M) = M(1)$ is the [forgetful functor](c:forgetful-functor).

conclusion: For all $n, m$ the map $\Phi\colon T(n, m) \to \mathrm{Nat}(U^n, U^m)$ is bijective and respects composition, so $T \cong T_U$.

proofs.name: Yoneda lemma
proofs.slogan: The free models $T(n, -)$ represent the powers of $U$, so natural operations on $U$ are morphisms of $T$ by the Yoneda lemma.
proofs.scope: Set-valued models of a one-sorted Lawvere theory. The proof gives $T(n, m) \cong \mathrm{Nat}(U^n, U^m)$ for all $n, m$; enriched and many-sorted versions are not covered.

roles.why: Finite products with objects $1^n$ make hom functors models and give $M(n) \cong U(M)^n$.
Models are functors, so $M(t)$ acts, and $\mathrm{Mod}(T)$ is a full subcategory where Yoneda applies.

steps.slogan: Identify the free models $F_n = T(n, -)$ and the isomorphism $M(n) \cong U(M)^n$.
steps.detail: A hom functor preserves products, so the [representable](c:representable-functor) functor $F_n = T(n, -)$ is a model. Since $\mathrm{Mod}(T)$ is a full subcategory of functors, Yoneda gives $\mathrm{Hom}(F_n, M) \cong M(n)$. A model preserves the product $n = 1^n$, so $M(n) \cong U(M)^n$ naturally in $M$.

steps.slogan: Define $\Phi$ and check that it respects composition.
steps.detail: A morphism $t\colon n \to m$ gives, for each model $M$, the function $M(t)\colon U(M)^n \to U(M)^m$. It is natural in $M$, since morphisms of models are [natural transformations](c:natural-transformation). Each $M$ is a functor, so $\Phi(s \circ t) = \Phi(s) \circ \Phi(t)$ and $\Phi(\mathrm{id}) = \mathrm{id}$.

steps.slogan: Read a morphism off a natural transformation at the generic tuple.
steps.detail: Let $\alpha\colon U^n \to U^m$ be natural. The element $\iota = \mathrm{id}_n \in F_n(n) \cong U(F_n)^n$ is the generic $n$-tuple. Put $\Psi(\alpha) = \alpha_{F_n}(\iota) \in U(F_n)^m \cong F_n(m) = T(n, m)$.

steps.slogan: Show that reading off the generic tuple of $\Phi(t)$ returns $t$.
steps.detail: For $t \in T(n, m)$, $\Phi(t)_{F_n}(\iota) = F_n(t)(\mathrm{id}_n) = t \circ \mathrm{id}_n = t$, because $F_n(t)$ is composition with $t$. So $\Psi(\Phi(t)) = t$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\Phi(\Psi(\alpha)) = \alpha$ by the Yoneda lemma and naturality.
steps.detail: Let $t = \Psi(\alpha)$, let $M$ be a model and $x \in U(M)^n \cong M(n)$. By Yoneda some $h\colon F_n \to M$ has $U(h)^n(\iota) = x$. Naturality of $\alpha$ and of $h$ give $\alpha_M(x) = U(h)^m(t) = h_m(t) = M(t)(h_n(\mathrm{id}_n)) = M(t)(x)$. So $\alpha = \Phi(t)$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $T$ is isomorphic to the theory $T_U$ of natural operations on $U$.
steps.detail: By the two previous steps $\Phi$ is a bijection on every hom set. It is functorial and the identity on objects, so it is an isomorphism of categories $T \to T_U$, where $T_U(n, m) = \mathrm{Nat}(U^n, U^m)$.

concepts.c:lawvere-theory: The theory $T$ is the category whose morphisms are the operations to recover.
concepts.c:forgetful-functor: The functor $U$ is the only data from which the operations are read.
concepts.c:algebraic-theory: The conclusion recovers the algebraic theory from its models and $U$.
concepts.c:representable-functor: The free models are representable functors, so Yoneda applies to them.
concepts.c:natural-transformation: Natural transformations of powers of $U$ are the operations that $\Phi$ matches with morphisms of $T$.

source.note: Two uses of the Yoneda lemma, as in F. W. Lawvere, Functorial Semantics of Algebraic Theories (thesis 1963; Reprints in Theory and Applications of Categories 5, 2004).
